topic: program repair; patch correctness and evaluation
status: established methodological risk; not a novel claim from this historical cell
claim: Patch success is conditional on the defect class, correctness oracle, benchmark, and intended use (recommendation versus fully automatic repair). A test-suite-passing patch is not automatically semantically correct, and a single correctness criterion does not fit every repair scenario.
positive_evidence: The 2014 essay distinguishes correctness, understandability, and completeness and explains how these criteria differ between repair recommendation and fully automatic/runtime repair.
A QuixBugs study reports 338 plausible patches, 53.3% of which were manually judged overfitting.
A 2019 11-tool, five-benchmark experiment reports patches for 21% of benchmark bugs overall; the rate was 47% for Defects4J and 10–30% for other benchmarks.

A later patch-assessment study found 10 of 97 semantically-equivalent-to-human patches previously claimed correct were overfitting, while also identifying false positives when generated tests violate implicit preconditions.
counterevidence: Later studies develop scalable automated patch assessment and report it can identify many overfitting patches; the problem is tractable in some settings.
These studies use selected Java benchmarks/tools and do not establish a universal overfitting rate or invalidate test-suite adequacy as a scoped engineering measure.

sources.title: Empirical Review of Java Program Repair Tools: A Large-Scale Experiment on 2,141 Bugs and 23,551 Repair Attempts
Automated Patch Assessment for Program Repair at Scale
sources.sections: abstract; §§4.3–4.4 manual disagreement and assessment false positives

falsifiable_test: For a preregistered set of defect classes, compare generated patches under the original test suite, hidden/specification-derived tests, differential tests, and blinded maintainer review. Stratify by recommendation versus auto-commit use and benchmark. Report plausible-patch rate, semantically correct rate, false-positive/false-negative rates, and reviewer agreement. The lead weakens if these oracles and intended-use strata yield materially equivalent conclusions across independent repositories.
limitations: Targeted synthesis of one conceptual essay and selected empirical studies, not a systematic review or pooled estimate. Java benchmark results do not generalize automatically to all languages, domains, or repair systems.

status: bounded cross-paper assurance lead; medical deployment efficacy not established
claim: The sampled medical-device paper demonstrates verified-pattern emulation in a simulator and one physical pump scenario, not end-to-end clinical safety. Formal guarantees remain conditional on timing, adapters, device behavior, and the covered safety pattern. Later CPS work likewise argues that simulation fidelity, scenario coverage, traceability, hardware-in-the-loop, and field tests matter; this is adjacent-domain support, not direct medical-device evidence.
positive_evidence: The pacemaker case uses a Java simulator and reports mostly sub-0.1-second jitter with rare values above 0.2 seconds on one stated machine/software configuration.
The physical syringe-pump case checks one execution using coarse scale readings against selected bolus duration/frequency constraints.
The authors explicitly exclude network-disconnection/open-loop safety and state the verified command-shaper pattern does not cover all device safety concerns.
A later CPS/sUAS framework paper identifies fidelity, scenario coverage, requirement-to-test traceability, and safety-analysis integration as gaps and calls its own results preliminary.
counterevidence: The formal pattern is verified under its formal assumptions; the physical pump demonstration shows the logical model can be connected to actual hardware in at least one case.
The later CPS evidence focuses on sUAS/robotics, so it cannot establish the size or existence of the same deployment gap in medical devices.

sources.title: Distributed Real-Time Emulation of Formally-Defined Patterns for Safe Medical Device Control
Coupled Requirements-driven Testing of CPS: From Simulation To Reality
sources.sections: abstract and framework motivation; adjacent sUAS/robotics counterevidence

falsifiable_test: For one formally specified safety controller, run the same requirements through formal proof, generated adapter/code, hardware-in-the-loop, and fault-injected field-like tests. Predeclare timing bounds and network/device failure modes, measure requirement coverage and violation detection, and compare model predictions with physical traces. The lead weakens if proof assumptions are shown to cover these operational variations and independent physical tests find no uncovered hazards.
limitations: One 2010 medical-device paper and one adjacent 2024 CPS proposal. No clinical deployment or prospective safety-outcome data were audited; the cross-domain analogy is a research lead only.

status: bounded methodological lead; effectiveness untested in the sampled framework paper
claim: A component taxonomy can make requirements-engineering methods easier to describe and compare, but taxonomy completeness does not demonstrate that a method improves stakeholder decisions or downstream outcomes. The sampled framework explicitly leaves systematic validation open and limits what its classification can decide.
positive_evidence: The 2012 paper defines five REM components and proposes the framework for analysis, teaching, extension, design, and validation.

It names systematic REM validation as a research challenge and states that the classification is limited: it offers a checklist but does not determine which concepts are relevant or prescribe a complete validation method.
counterevidence: The framework points to existing component-specific validation methods and can be useful as a design/analysis scaffold; lack of an effectiveness experiment does not show the framework is ineffective.
One conceptual framework paper cannot establish the state of all REM validation research.

sources.title: Requirements Engineering Methods: A Classification Framework and Research Challenges

falsifiable_test: Select one REM and preregister a comparison against an explicit baseline with independent stakeholders. Measure requirement coverage, inconsistency detection, traceability, decision quality, and task time across representative scenarios. The lead weakens if the component taxonomy alone predicts these outcomes and improves them across independent stakeholder groups.
limitations: Single conceptual paper; no systematic review of all requirements-engineering method evaluations was performed in this batch.
